title: Rumbly Learns to See
markdown:
Moonbeams drifted through the museum windows and laid sleepy stripes on the polished floor. Asha the museum helper hummed the tune she always used while putting the day’s quiet discoveries away. Labels went into their drawers. A beetle pin was set straight. Her garden patch, outside the back door, was a pride: blushing tomatoes, shy lavender, a pumpkin that had begun to think of itself as furniture. Lately a wobble had entered it.

Rumbly, her new helper robot — smooth metal, a soft melodic whir — was meant to make the soil easier. Arms for gentle water and weed. It still moved in determined straight lines, a little too much like a runaway beetle, and those lines found her terracotta pots. Soil tumbled. Seedlings scattered. Asha sighed like rustling leaves, righted the pots, and felt a quiet worry for Rumbly’s unawareness and the tremble in her own hands. She loved the patch. She loved Rumbly. The bumps sat between.

Tumble the goat, who liked the garden after hours, nibbled a dandelion and watched. “Maa?” when a pot wobbled. He knew those pots promised clover and juicy roots. His tail flicked concern. He did not offer to herd the robot. He had tried once. Rumbly had not understood goats.

One evening the last sun painted lavender and rose. Rumbly aimed around a grand pumpkin, whir more determined, and found the basil pot instead. Asha’s fingers twitched to catch. The terracotta thudded. Basil leaves shook as if they had been told a secret they did not like.

Professor Imani’s voice arrived warm as afternoon. “Rather direct in its journey.”

Imani loved the patch for every bloom and bee. She watched Rumbly pause, blue and green lights blinking as if thinking. “It sees the path in front, not what waits beside. It isn’t looking around.”

Asha’s brow made leaf-lines. “I wish it would swerve. Or stop. The way Tumble does when the grass smells especially sweet.”

“Rumbly has sensors — little electronic eyes and ears. They need to be told what to look for, and what to do when they find it. A little more to think with.”

Together they worked at the back bench: Asha’s hands that knew every petal, Imani’s words that made the console feel like a garden tool. They taught the sensors the edges of pots, the beanstalks reaching, the pumpkin curves like sleeping giants. Asha held a pot at arm’s length so Rumbly’s lights could learn the rim. Then new instructions, quiet as secrets: If you see a pot, turn left. If you see a vine, go slowly forward and around.

Rumbly’s whir softened, more musical. The first test was only as far as the pumpkin. It glided, paused, turned left of the basil as if the pot had spoken. Tumble bleated approval from the fence. Asha clapped softly and then put her hands in her pockets so she would not clap again and startle the lettuce.

They sent it the long way: tomatoes, lavender, the row of sleeping seedlings. If pot, left. If vine, slow and around. The path became a curve, a dancing leaf. Soil stayed in its pots. Imani whispered, wonder without a sermon, “Decisions. If this, then that.”

Rumbly watered sleeping lettuce with a precise spray. The moon, higher, made dew into small lamps. The gate lights glowed like tired fireflies. Asha did not ask the night what other wonders science held. She watched one more clean pass between basil and pumpkin, then switched Rumbly to rest. The blue and green lights dimmed in order, like a sentence finishing. Tumble claimed the dandelion he had been saving. The pots, for the first time that week, stayed where they had been put.
